walkthroughs.body_html:
Acids, Bases & Salts — a core area of GCSE Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Acids, Bases & Salts brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Acids, Bases & Salts.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Moving from pH 3 to pH 5 means H⁺ concentration:
options: doubles
halves
increases 100x
decreases 100x

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid?
options: Strong and concentrated mean the same thing for acids.
Neutralisation always produces a solution with pH 0.
A strong acid fully dissociates in water; a concentrated acid has a high amount of acid per volume — these are independent properties.
A strong acid is one that has been heated to higher temperature.

mcqs.q: When an acid neutralises an alkali, what is the pH of the resulting solution?
options: Neutralisation always produces a solution with pH exactly 7 regardless of the acid and base used.
Chemical shift is the mass of the molecule divided by 1000.
Approximately 7 if equivalent amounts of strong acid and strong alkali react — but it varies with strength.
Neutralisation always produces a solution with pH 0.

mcqs.q: What does an NMR chemical shift (δ, in ppm) actually measure?
options: The position of a peak RELATIVE to TMS (tetramethylsilane, δ = 0), normalised by the spectrometer frequency.
Chemical shift is the mass of the molecule divided by 1000.
A strong acid is one that has been heated to higher temperature.
Chemical shift is the absolute resonance frequency of the nucleus in Hz.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Neutral”?
options: Soluble base that produces OH⁻ ions in solution. pH > 7.
Solution with pH 7; equal H⁺ and OH⁻, e.g. pure water.
Substance that produces H⁺ ions in solution. pH < 7.
0 (strong acid) to 14 (strong alkali); each step is a 10× change in H⁺ concentration.
